title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XIX
paragraphs:
“L’ altra vedete ch’ha fatto alla guancia
Della sua palma, sospirando, letto.”
—_Purgatorio_, vii.

While George the Fourth still reigned over Windsor's private world, the Duke of Wellington was Prime Minister, and Mr. Vincy was mayor of Middlemarch's old corporation, Mrs. Casaubon, born Dorothea Brooke, went to Rome on her honeymoon. The world then had forty years less knowledge of good and evil than it has now. Travelers seldom carried a thorough understanding of Christian art, either in their heads or in their pockets. Even the day's most brilliant English critic mistook the flower-filled tomb of the Virgin after her Assumption for an ornamental vase invented by the painter. Romanticism, which has helped fill some dull empty spaces with love and knowledge, had not yet spread its leaven through the age and entered everyone's daily food. In Rome it was still fermenting as a distinct and vigorous enthusiasm among certain long-haired German artists. Young people from other nations who worked or idled near them were sometimes swept into the growing movement.

One fine morning a young man with abundant curls, though not excessively long hair, and otherwise English in appearance, had just turned from the Belvedere Torso in the Vatican. From the adjoining circular vestibule he was looking out at the magnificent mountain view. He was so absorbed that he did not notice a lively, dark-eyed German approaching. The German laid a hand on his shoulder and said in a strong accent, “Come quickly, before she changes her pose!”

The call met a ready response. The two hurried lightly past the Meleager towards the hall containing the reclining Ariadne, then known as Cleopatra. She lay in the marble luxuriance of her beauty, drapery folding about her with the gentle ease of petals. They arrived just in time to see another figure standing against a pedestal near the statue: a living, blooming girl, her form unembarrassed by comparison with Ariadne, dressed in plain gray like a Quaker. Her long cloak, fastened at the neck, was thrown back from her arms. One beautiful bare hand supported her cheek, pushing back slightly the white beaver bonnet that made a sort of halo around her face and simply braided dark-brown hair. She was not looking at the sculpture and probably was not thinking about it. Her large eyes rested dreamily on a shaft of sunlight across the floor. Then she became aware of the two strangers who had suddenly stopped as though to study the Cleopatra. Without looking at them, she immediately turned away to join a maid and a traveling attendant who were lingering farther down the hall.

“What do you think of that for a splendid contrast?” the German asked, searching his friend's face for answering admiration but continuing rapidly without waiting for a reply. “There lies ancient beauty, not corpse-like even in death, but caught in complete satisfaction with its own sensuous perfection. And here stands living, breathing beauty, carrying the consciousness of centuries of Christianity in her heart. But she ought to wear a nun's habit. She almost looks like what you call a Quaker. I'd paint her as a nun. She's married, though. I saw the wedding ring on that wonderful left hand; otherwise I'd have taken the sallow clergyman for her father. I saw him leave her some time ago, and just now I found her in that magnificent pose. Think of it! Perhaps he's rich and would like her portrait painted. Ah, no use gazing after her—there she goes! Let's follow her home!”
“No, no,” his companion said with a slight frown.
“You're behaving strangely, Ladislaw. You look thunderstruck. Do you know her?”
“I know she's married to my cousin,” said Will Ladislaw, walking slowly down the hall, preoccupied, while his German friend stayed beside him and watched eagerly.
“What, the clergyman? He looks more like an uncle—a more useful relation.”
“He isn't my uncle. I told you, he's my second cousin,” Ladislaw said irritably.
“Very well, very well. Don't snap. You're not angry because I think Mrs. Second Cousin the most perfect young Madonna I've ever seen?”

“Angry? Don't be absurd. I've only seen her once before, for a couple of minutes, when my cousin introduced us just before I left England. They weren't married then. I didn't know they were coming to Rome.”
“But now you'll visit them. You can find their address, since you know the name. Shall we try the post office? And you could mention the portrait.”
“Damn it, Naumann! I don't know what I'll do. I'm not as shameless as you.”

“Bah! That's because you're a dabbler, an amateur. If you were an artist, you'd see Mistress Second Cousin as classical form brought to life by Christian feeling—a kind of Christian Antigone, sensuous strength governed by spiritual passion.”

“Yes, and you'd think your painting her was the main purpose of her existence: divinity reaching a higher perfection and almost spending itself in the effort to cover your little canvas. Call me an amateur if you like. I DON'T believe the whole universe is straining towards the obscure meaning of your pictures.”

“But it is, my dear fellow, insofar as it strains through me, Adolf Naumann. That is indisputable,” said the good-natured painter, laying a hand on Ladislaw's shoulder, entirely untroubled by the inexplicable irritation in his voice. “Look! My existence presupposes the existence of the whole universe, doesn't it? My purpose is to paint. As a painter, I have a positively inspired conception of your great-aunt or second grandmother as a subject. Therefore the universe is striving towards that picture through the particular hook or claw it has extended in the form of me. Isn't that so?”
“But what if another claw, in the form of me, is trying to prevent it? That makes the case less simple.”
“Not at all. Whatever the struggle produces, a picture or no picture, the result is the same thing, logically.”
Will could not resist such unshakable good humor. The cloud on his face dissolved into sunny laughter.
“Come, my friend, you'll help?” Naumann asked hopefully.

“No, Naumann, it's nonsense. English ladies aren't available to everyone as models. And you're trying to express too much in paint. All you'd produce would be a better or worse portrait with a background every connoisseur would praise or blame for a different reason. What is a woman's portrait, after all? Your painting and sculpture are poor things. They muddle and deaden our ideas instead of elevating them. Language is a finer medium.”
“Yes, for people who can't paint,” said Naumann. “There you're perfectly right. I didn't advise you to paint, my friend.”
The friendly artist had a sting, but Ladislaw chose not to seem wounded. He continued as though he had not heard.

“Language creates a fuller image, improved by its very vagueness. True vision is inward, after all. A painting stares back at you with insistent imperfection. I feel that especially in pictures of women. As if a woman were nothing but a colored surface! You have to wait for movement and tone. Even their breathing differs. They change from moment to moment. Take the woman you just saw: how would you paint her voice? Yet her voice is far more divine than anything you've seen of her.”
“I understand, I understand. You're jealous. No man may presume he can paint your ideal. This is serious, my friend! Your great-aunt! The Nephew as Uncle, turned tragic—monstrous!”
“We'll quarrel, Naumann, if you call that lady my aunt again.”
“What should I call her, then?”
“Mrs. Casaubon.”
“Good. Suppose I get to know her despite you, and discover she'd very much like to be painted?”

“Yes, suppose!” Will Ladislaw said in a scornful undertone meant to end the subject. He knew ridiculously small things were irritating him, half of them of his own making. Why was he making such a fuss about Mrs. Casaubon? Yet he felt as if something concerning her had happened to him. Some people continually create clashes and complications for themselves in dramas no one else is prepared to perform with them. Their sensitivities collide with objects that remain innocently still.
